title: Passengers Recount Terror as Air India Phuket-Delhi Flight Plunges 300 Feet
excerpt: At least 12 people were injured when Air India flight AI2379 hit severe turbulence mid-cruise, prompting India's aviation regulator to open a formal investigation and seize the aircraft's black boxes.
body:
• Air India flight AI2379, an Airbus A320neo carrying 137 passengers and 8 crew from Phuket to Delhi, plunged approximately 300 feet during cruise on Tuesday after encountering severe turbulence.
  • At least 12 people — eight passengers and four crew members — were injured and taken to hospital; India's DGCA confirmed one cabin crew member suffered a "severe injury."
  • Authorities have secured the aircraft's Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder and launched a formal investigation into the incident.
  • Shaken passengers described being thrown from their seats while many on board were asleep, with one planning legal action against the airline.

Mid-Air Plunge Catches Sleeping Passengers Off Guard

An Air India Airbus A320neo plummeted roughly 300 feet during cruise altitude on Tuesday, throwing passengers and crew around the cabin approximately 90 minutes after departing Phuket, Thailand, for Delhi.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=gzBN47OiFSA

Flight AI2379, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew members, landed safely at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport at around 11 a.m. local time (5:37 a.m. GMT), according to Reuters. Emergency services were waiting on the tarmac as the aircraft touched down.

Many passengers were reportedly asleep when the aircraft suddenly tilted and began shaking violently for two to three minutes. Footage circulating on social media showed visible cracks in the cabin ceiling following the plunge.

"The aircraft seemed to be moving normally but suddenly the turbulence began. I saw my sister thrown into the air from her seat. My mother was knocked on her head. My phone fell."

— Passenger speaking to ANI

Injuries and Immediate Response

India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation confirmed that eight passengers and four crew members were injured, with at least one cabin crew member sustaining what the regulator classified as a "severe injury." The New York Post reported the total number of injured at 14, citing additional passengers with minor complaints.

Video from the airport showed at least one injured person being wheeled out on a gurney and loaded into an ambulance with a head injury. Others were seen leaving in wheelchairs. The injured were taken to the Medanta medical centre and the airport's own medical facility for evaluation.

One passenger told ANI that a male traveler seated behind her had blood on his face after the incident. "We thought we would die. It was really scary. I was shaking and crying," she said. Another passenger told reporters they are planning to take legal action against Air India.

Investigation Launched, Black Boxes Seized

Indian authorities moved quickly, securing the aircraft's Flight Data Recorder and Cockpit Voice Recorder for examination, the government said on Tuesday. The 7-year-old Airbus jet has been grounded pending the probe's preliminary findings.

Air India characterized the incident as a "brief in-flight turbulence-related event during cruise, resulting in a momentary change in altitude," adding that none of the injuries were serious — a claim at odds with the DGCA's own classification of at least one crew injury as severe.

"A small number of passengers and crew members with minor injuries requiring medical assessment have been taken to a medical facility at the airport for precautionary examination and care," the airline said in a statement to the Indian Express. Airbus did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Heightened Scrutiny for Air India

The turbulence incident comes at a sensitive time for Air India. Just over a year ago, London-bound Air India flight AI171 crashed 32 seconds after takeoff from Ahmedabad Airport in Gujarat, killing 241 people on board — all but one sole surviving passenger — and 19 on the ground.

That disaster, one of India's worst aviation tragedies, had already placed the Tata Group-owned carrier under intense regulatory and public scrutiny. Tuesday's incident, while far less severe in outcome, is likely to renew questions about maintenance standards and safety protocols across the airline's fleet.

What It Means for Indian Travelers Abroad

For the thousands of Indian diaspora members who regularly fly Air India on routes connecting South and Southeast Asia, the incident is a stark reminder of the risks of severe turbulence — a phenomenon aviation experts say is becoming more frequent due to climate change. The Phuket-Delhi route is popular among Indian tourists and the diaspora community in Thailand.

The DGCA's investigation will determine whether the altitude loss was caused purely by atmospheric conditions or if any mechanical or procedural factors contributed. Results from the black box analysis are expected in the coming weeks.
nri_angle: The Phuket-Delhi route is heavily used by Indian diaspora and tourists in Southeast Asia, and the incident raises safety concerns for frequent flyers on Air India's regional network.
